title: Four strengths
hookLine: aspiration, steadiness, joy and rest: four supports for effort (Bodhicaryavatara 7)
tomorrow: rested and ready. so how do you actually start?

cards: Run a finger along a bonsai's trunk in winter and nothing seems to be happening. No new shoots. No wiring, no trimming.
The gardener leaves it alone. To a beginner it looks like neglect. To the tree, it's how next spring gets made.
Gardeners call the season dormant. It sounds like sleeping. It's closer to gathering.
Shantideva, writing about effort, says something a hustle feed would never print: one of effort's strengths is rest.

teach.b: Halfway through the effort chapter, he names the supports that keep effort going, like the divisions of an army. First, aspiration, chanda in Sanskrit: wanting the good, feeling its pull.
Second, steadiness: a quiet confidence that you can finish what you start. Third, joy: pleasure in the work itself, the delight from two days ago. And fourth, the surprising one: letting go.
When your strength is spent, set the task down, to pick it up again later. When it's finished, release it and turn to the next. Feel them in the body and they make sense.
Steadiness is feet flat on the floor.
And rest is the long exhale after lifting something heavy, the moment the shoulders drop. Without that last one, the other three wear out. Aspiration with no rest turns into anxiety.
Steadiness with no rest turns stubborn. Even joy, pushed past its limit, goes flat. Shantideva doesn't treat rest as a prize for being good, or a weakness to hide.
He lists it right beside aspiration and joy. The tree in winter isn't failing at being a tree.

how: Buddhist teachers often present Shantideva's supports for effort as a balance of drive and release; many retreats build rest periods into a day of practice.

s: Shantideva treats rest as a reward you earn only when everything is finished
he says set the task down when strength is spent, to take it up again later.
joy is one of the supports Shantideva names for effort

games.q: you've finished a long shift, and there's an hour left before bed. by Shantideva's supports, what's the strong move?
o: set the work down fully and rest, knowing you'll pick it up again.
push on another hour; rest is for when everything is done.
spend the hour planning everything left so nothing slips.
games.why: letting go when strength is spent is one of effort's supports. the task waits; you come back to it stronger.

practice: Make one small effort with your body: press your palms together firmly, or lift your shoulders toward your ears, and hold it through one full breath. Then let it all go at once, and stay inside the letting go.
Feel what rest is like when it comes right after work.

wordCard.voice: Four strengths: Shantideva's supports for effort, aspiration, steadiness, joy and letting go. The last one is rest.

orig.note: Sanskrit: strength, force; Shantideva's word for these supports of effort.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: rest is a strength, and the tree in winter is still a tree. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 7.31-7.32 (the supports of effort: aspiration, steadfastness, joy, letting go); 7.66-7.67 (set it down when strength wanes; when done, turn to the next)
